Beállítom Az M3-ason történt buszbaleset sérültjeinek első csoportja hétfő este tér vissza Lengyelországba, írja a PolsatNews . Adam Szłapka kormányszóvivő szerint mintegy 20 emberről van szó. Szłapka egy sajtótájékoztatón azt mondta: az orvosok most felmérik a sérültek állapotát, és azt vizsgálják, hogy kik azok, akik elsőként hazarepülhetnek. A lengyel hadsereg repülőgépeket biztosított a szállításhoz. A szóvivő azt is mondta, hogy Varsó felé útközben Rzeszówban leszáll a gép, így akiknek további kórházi ellátásra van szükségük, az otthonukhoz közelebb kaphatják meg a szükséges kezelést. A busz utasai a Kárpátaljai vajdaságban található Strzyżów és környékének lakói voltak. A szóvivő hozzátette, hogy a vajdasági hivatal szervezési és pszichológiai segítséget nyújt az érintetteknek. „Azok számára, akik súlyosabb állapotban vannak, és nem tudnak az első csoporttal hazatérni, katonai kórházat jelöltünk ki. Azoknak pedig, akiknek olyan súlyos az állapotuk, hogy a hazaszállítás ilyen módon nehéz lenne, az Egészségügyi Minisztérium speciális egészségügyi szállító repülőgépet biztosít” – mondta Szłapka. „Az orvosok egyeztetnek a magyar kollégáikkal és magukkal a sérültekkel is. Ezek alapján dől majd el, hogy az adott sérült állapota lehetővé teszi-e, hogy még ma repülővel hazaszállítsák, vagy egy kicsit tovább kell maradnia Magyarországon” – mondta Wojciech Zajączkowski lengyel külügyminiszter-helyettes a TVN24 szerint . Azt mondta, hogy a Lengyelországba tartó repülőgép Budapestről vagy Debrecenből indul majd. „Azt mérlegeljük, hogyan tudjuk ezt logisztikailag megszervezni. Az is kérdés, hogy a négy helyszínről hol tudjuk a lehető leggyorsabban összegyűjteni a sérülteket” – mondta. A Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén Vármegyei Központi Kórház és Egyetemi Oktatókórház beszámolt a vasárnapi balesetben megsérült lengyelek állapotáról. Összesen kilenc embert szállítottak ebbe a kórházba. Két beteg nagyon súlyos állapotban van, őket az aneszteziológiai és intenzív terápiás osztályon kezelik. „Állapotuk súlyos és életveszélyes, de jelenleg stabil” – közölte a kórház. Hozzátették, hogy „mindkét betegnek műtéti beavatkozásra van szüksége”. Egy ember gerincsérüléssel fekszik az idegsebészeti osztályon. „Már ma átszállítható további kórházi kezelésre, jelenlegi állapota lehetővé teszi a szállítást” – közölte a kórház. Öt beteget a traumatológiai osztályon kezelnek. A közlemény szerint „sérüléseik jellegének és súlyosságának megfelelő ellátásban részesülnek”. A kilencedik, vasárnap kórházba szállított beteg „járóbeteg-ellátást követően távozott” az intézményből. Egy zarándoklat résztvevői utaztak hazafelé azon a lengyel turistabuszon, ami egyelőre tisztázatlan okból letért az útról és árokba borult az M3-as autópályán vasárnap éjjel 1 órakor, a rendőrség hivatalos tájékoztatása szerint a balesetben tizenketten meghaltak . A busz utasai lengyel állampolgárok voltak. Maciej Wewiór külügyi szóvivő vasárnap azt mondta, hét sérült állapota nagyon súlyos, további mintegy 40 személy könnyebb sérüléseket szenvedett. https://www.politico.eu/article/diplomat.text: A senior diplomat will try to form a new government as Romania’s prime minister, in an attempt to end a five-month stalemate that threatens the country’s economic and political stability. President Nicușor Dan named Luca Niculescu, secretary of state in the foreign ministry, as prime minister-designate on Monday. He is the fourth candidate tasked with leading a government since the coalition collapsed in May. To be confirmed in the role, Niculescu will need to win a vote in Romania’s parliament within 10 days to show he has majority support for his new ministerial team and their program for government. Advertisement Advertisement His task is formidable: Amid bitter divisions between the parties, lawmakers rejected two of Dan’s previous nominees, and a third didn’t even make that far. Dan made his announcement after holding talks with the parties at Cotroceni Palace on Monday afternoon. After three previous candidates failed, the president is already facing calls to dissolve parliament for an unprecedented snap election. But he is reluctant to do so, fearing it would bring a far-right euroskeptic opposition party closer to power. “My proposal for the position of prime minister is Luca Niculescu, a man who, as a diplomat, knows how to harmonize different positions,” Dan said on Monday evening. “It is necessary for Romania to have a government as soon as possible, because there are institutions that need rectification, and there is a need for a budget for next year. Prolonging the uncertainty will have effects on the lives of Romanians.” One politician who refused to take part in talks with Dan on Monday was George Simion, leader of the hard-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians party, which currently leads opinion polls . Simion — who challenged Dan for the presidency last year — reiterated his demand for an election to end the chaos. The president confirmed that the new government would have no place for parties that are anti-Western — which is his code for far-right groups, especially AUR. “I have the guarantee that a government with Luca Niculescu will maintain Romania’s pro-Western direction and will respect the financial targets and all the commitments that Romania has undertaken,” he said. Dan said the uncertainty was affecting exchange rates, interest rates and investments in Romania. Over the past four years, Niculescu has led Romania’s accession process to the OECD, a major milestone in the country’s development. Dan said his candidate would have the freedom to decide whether the government was “political or technocratic.” Accepting the nomination, Niculescu said Romania was grappling with a “long” period of uncertainty at a difficult time. “The first mission will be to build a parliamentary majority that will vote for a government that will be deeply anchored in Romania’s European and Euro-Atlantic direction,” he said. “I will have discussions with the parliamentary parties to build this majority and to agree on a realistic governing program.” Advertisement Advertisement

All photographs by Korbinian Leo Kramer Photograph: Leo Kramer Amid blackouts, artillery fire and the onslaught of Russian drone attacks, the Richelievsky in Kherson provides a refuge for those with nowhere else to go By Korbinian Leo Kramer in Kherson Supported by About this content Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T here is one important rule in the Richelievsky, Kherson’s last functioning hotel: close the curtains before dusk. Less than a kilometre away lies the Dnipro, the river that has formed the frontline since Ukrainian forces liberated Kherson in November 2022; Moscow’s troops are on the opposite bank. In a city where Russian drone operators hunt civilians in what is now widely known as the “human safari”, even a sliver of light escaping through a window may be enough to reveal someone’s location after dark. View image in fullscreen Hotel manager Yevhen Emtsov, 46, in the building’s former conference room In the lobby, Yevhen Emtsov, the hotel’s manager, sits at a small round table almost buried beneath papers. Outside, explosions punctuate the evening, joined at intervals by the mechanical hum of drones patrolling the streets in the red zone. Inside, residents pass through, pausing with questions and requests at the table that now serves as Emtsov’s office. In more peaceful times, the Richelievsky accommodated tourists and business travellers attending conferences. The three-star hotel belonged to a different Kherson, one in which the river drew visitors rather than marking a frontline. View image in fullscreen Anti-drone nets stretch above Ushakova Street. More than 2,000 Russian drones are detected over Kherson in an average week, according to official figures But in March 2022, as Russian forces closed in, Emtsov began taking in people fleeing heavily shelled communities along the Dnipro without waiting for the hotel owners’ approval. By the time the city came under occupation, the building had already begun its transformation from a commercial hotel into a refuge. View image in fullscreen Smoke rises over the rooftops of Kherson’s red zone, viewed from the sixth floor of the Richelievsky In the months that followed the invasion, between 200 and 300 people were staying, far beyond its intended maximum capacity of 120. Russian patrols would enter the building, questioning residents and recording their fingerprints. “Imagine you are sitting at home, strangers come in and begin doing whatever they want,” Emtsov says. Today, the hotel is home to 41 displaced people, with rooms and three meals a day provided free of charge. “People come to us,” Emtsov says. “You can sleep here today, and tomorrow we will see. Nobody sleeps on the street. Nobody.” View image in fullscreen Graffiti above a pedestrian underpass. Many of those who remain give personal reasons: an elderly relative, a job or animal left behind, or simply the difficulty of starting again in an unfamiliar place It is close to midnight when the power cuts out, leaving the hotel and the city in complete darkness. “Drones and artillery can be heard throughout the night,” Emtsov says. “By morning, you will be able to smell the smoke.” Hours later, kept awake by the noise of bombing outside, I make my way towards the top of the building, where the seventh floor lies deserted. From up here, Kherson is almost entirely dark, its streets and buildings barely distinguishable in the blackout. Brief flashes flare among the stars, while explosions and the buzz of drones carry through the night. When daylight returns, the building shows no sign of stirring. At this hour, the Richelievsky feels like a ghost hotel, mirroring the emptied neighbourhoods of Kherson’s red zone. View image in fullscreen ‘My home is gone. Everything burned down. But I have a roof over my head,’ says Natalia Yastreb, 58, a hotel resident who also works in the kitchen The first people to emerge are in the hotel kitchen: Natalia Yastreb and Iryna Rybalchenko reheat fishcakes and stew from the previous evening. Residents drift wearily into the adjoining dining room with their plates, exchanging few words as detonations continue outside. View image in fullscreen Nina Tsokurenko, 78, and her husband, Viktor, 83, have been staying across two rooms at the Richelievsky for six months While some residents have already left for work, Nina and Viktor Tsokurenko begin the day in room 43 with exercises and tea. Since suffering a stroke, Viktor has struggled to speak. “There was a powerful explosion at one o’clock,” Nina says. “After that, I did not sleep again until morning.” Still, she offers coffee and honey; before the war, the couple kept bees. One floor below, four cats pad around room 37. Tatyana Nesterchuk, one of the hotel’s longest-standing residents, has returned from a shift at a laundry in Kherson’s Dniprovskyi district. The minibus journey to work takes her through some of the city’s most dangerous streets, with an emergency bag always at her side. “It is like a one-way road,” she says. “You do not know whether you will return. Before setting out, it is as though I am leaving a will behind.” View image in fullscreen Tatyana Nesterchuk, 54, arrived at the Richelievsky with her family in March 2022. Doctors advised against moving her bedridden mother. ‘I had to choose: leave her here and go somewhere safer, or stay with her. Of course, I stayed,’ she says. Her mother died at the hotel in May, aged 81 When warnings of incoming guided aerial bombs reach the hotel, she heads to the shelter with family photographs and other keepsakes packed into her suitcase, which weighs about 10kg. “It is heavy,” she says. “My son tells me to take half of it out. I tell him, ‘I can’t.’” Nesterchuk has been told that her house has since burned down. Even the fences are gone. “But the land, at least, will remain, I suppose.” She remembers drinking coffee on a small terrace before leaving for work or taking a hoe into the garden to tend fruit and vegetables. “I always loved the mornings at home,” she says. “The birds were singing. It was quiet and peaceful. There was no buzzing, no humming.” View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen From left: room 75 on the top floor after a Russian Grad rocket tore through it in February; a plate of pelmeni – meat-filled dumplings – on a kitchen windowsill after the cooks have finished for the day Another air raid siren cuts across the city. In room 54, Alisia Logvinenko, 11, the only child among the hotel’s residents, answers my knock. She speaks in a breathless rush that makes her difficult to follow. Her mother, Iryna, stands behind her. The 50-year-old tries to put the war into words a child can understand. “Someone wants to take away our home.” “To conquer a country,” Alisia adds. “Did I say that correctly?” “Yes, you did,” her mother says. When Iryna mentions the few friends they still have in Kherson, Alisia cuts in. “Not mine, hers.” Most of the children she knew before the war have left Kherson. “I don’t really miss them,” she says, opening her YouTube channel and turning the screen towards me. What makes her happy now, she says, is “lots of likes on my videos”. View image in fullscreen Svitlana Salii, 43, helps residents at the reception desk. She moved into the hotel with her family in December 2022. ‘I understand the people here because I’m going through the same pain,’ she says Before the invasion, Iryna had planned to take Alisia camping in Ukraine’s nature reserves. The landscape her daughter has learned to navigate instead is governed by a different set of rules. “Look at the sky. Listen and try to go where there are more trees and walls,” Iryna says. The hotel may offer a measure of shelter, but she has no illusions about its limits. “There is no feeling of safety anywhere.” Downstairs, Svitlana Salii, Emtsov’s right hand, is behind the reception desk when her phone rings. As she listens, her expression tightens. A Russian FPV drone has struck the van carrying the hotel’s manager and several helpers on their way back from collecting groceries. Outside, the mechanical hum rises and fades, and I find Emtsov and the others about 15 minutes away, gathered around the white Mercedes. “What can I tell you?” he says. “We heard the buzzing, saw the drone ahead and got out in time to take cover before it crashed into the vehicle.” View image in fullscreen Emtsov beside a car that was struck by a drone, part of its wing still lodged in the glass The attack is another reminder of what it costs to keep the place running. “As a hotel, we will not be able to operate. But as a hub, we will continue for as long as we have enough strength.” As conditions in Kherson continue to deteriorate, Emtsov is trying to find a way out of the city for Iryna and Alisia; charities are seeking a place for them in Odesa. For now, mother and daughter remain in room 54, behind curtains drawn before dusk. View image in fullscreen A burned-out car in Kherson’s red zone. With Kyiv requiring up to 360 interceptors for winter defense, and US stockpiles dipping below 1,700 due to operations in the Middle East, European allies are seeking to unlock southern European arsenals. by Kyiv Post | Oct. 10, 2026, 1:00 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Visitors queue to take a closer look at a Patriot missile launcher during Armed Forces Day at the Airbase in Laage, Germany, on June 06, 2026. (Photo by John MACDOUGALL / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip NATO and EU officials are lobbying Greece and Spain to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles nearing the end of their operational shelf life to Ukraine, The Telegraph reported. Athens and Madrid hold some of Europe’s largest national inventories of Patriot PAC-2 interceptors, weapons that Ukrainian defense planners urgently require to protect urban population centers and energy infrastructure from Russian ballistic and cruise missile strikes. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . President Volodymyr Zelensky previously stated that Ukrainian forces require between 300 and 360 Patriot interceptors to withstand anticipated winter bombardments. According to military records cited by The Telegraph, Greece holds at least 200 Patriot PAC-2 missiles whose certified 23-year operational lifespan is approaching expiration. While the exact quantity held in Spanish military depots remains classified, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares confirmed last month that Madrid would deliver five interceptors to Kyiv. Advertisement Allied defense coordinators argue that transferring aging munitions before they surpass statutory shelf limits represents a pragmatic solution for both donor nations and Ukraine. Patriot interceptors carry manufacturer-guaranteed shelf lives during which performance is certified; once that operational window elapses, the missiles must undergo expensive and logistically intensive factory recertifications. Other Topics of Interest Medvedev Warns Against Travel to Europe, Claims It Is ‘Targeting Russians’ Dmitry Medvedev urged Russians to avoid Europe following a pro-war blogger’s arrest in Montenegro and suggested detaining Western nationals for future exchanges. “We know that some countries have interceptor missiles that will expire soon,” EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas said during multilateral consultations in Ireland last month. “So it would be very good if they were transferred to Ukraine.” Global Patriot shortfalls and US-Iran conflict The diplomatic initiative to unlock southern European stockpiles arrives as Western defense planners confront severe bottlenecks in interceptor manufacturing, compounded by ongoing military operations involving the United States in the Middle East . Ukraine historically relies on a NATO-coordinated framework for roughly 95 percent of its Patriot interceptors, a mechanism under which European partner governments pool financial resources to purchase replacement missiles directly from American production lines. Advertisement However, heavy expenditure of surface-to-air missiles during the US conflict with Iran has precipitated a severe global inventory deficit. US military stockpiles of Patriot missiles have fallen to fewer than 1,700 units, fueling doubts among European allies regarding the Pentagon’s willingness to release additional interceptors from strategic reserves while active combat operations in the Middle East continue. With US supply lines backlogged by multi-year production lead times, Western defense coordinators have intensified efforts to identify existing surface-to-air missiles stored within European arsenals that can be deployed to Ukrainian batteries immediately without degrading the conventional defense readiness of donor nations. Eastern flank reinforcement The scramble to source interceptors for Ukraine coincides with expanding NATO deployments to protect the primary logistical conduits funneling Western military assistance across the Ukrainian border. On Tuesday, Oct. 6, the Swedish government announced that Sweden will deploy a Patriot air defense battery alongside approximately 100 military personnel to southeastern Poland in December. Advertisement The Swedish detachment, drawn from the Air Defence Regiment with support from the Blekinge Air Wing, will be stationed around Rzeszów, the principal transit hub through which international military aid and humanitarian cargo enter Ukraine. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson confirmed that the system – designated domestically as Air Defence System 103 – will operate under NATO Air Command as part of the alliance’s Integrated Air and Missile Defense network through the end of 2026, with planning underway to extend the mission into 2027. The ground battery supplements Swedish JAS 39 Gripen multirole fighters that integrated into NATO air policing over Poland earlier in October. The allied mission in Rzeszów aligns with broader moves by Warsaw to reinforce Poland’s eastern boundary, including the positioning of Polish Patriot units in the Lublin region to deter airspace incursions as Russian standoff strikes continue along the Ukrainian frontier.
